column4: In a blood-liability settlement, any portion pardoned by the claimant is followed by fair pursuit and gracious payment, and the arrangement is explicitly called a lightening and mercy; it closely models a creditor reducing a quantified due without abolishing justice.
A divorced woman's half-dowry remains due unless she or the holder of the marriage bond waives it, and waiving is nearer to piety; this is a precise financial claim voluntarily lowered by its owner.

Women receive their dowries as an entitlement, but may willingly remit part of it; the ayah distinguishes a due from its freehearted cancellation exactly as the section distinguishes debt from charitable remission.
Blood money must be delivered to the victim's family unless they relinquish it as charity, making the voluntary cancellation of a monetary liability itself ṣadaqah just as in 2:280.
After fixing equivalent retaliation as a right, the ayah calls waiving that right as charity an expiation; a claimant's measurable entitlement can thus become charitable release.

The final prayer joins capacity-limited obligation, a plea not to have a crushing burden laid upon the believers, and requests for pardon and forgiveness; these are the moral and bodily dimensions of the section's remitted liability in one ayah.
The sky is raised and the balance is set down: وَرَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ pairs the section's raising and lowering verbs with an instrument of exact accounting.
The command not to transgress in the balance states the ethical limit governing the account whose scale is set down in 55:7.
Upholding weight with justice and not diminishing the balance gives exact commercial content to the section's image of a claim being measured and reduced.
People are told to be mindful as far as they are able and to spend, while guarding against their own stinginess; 64:17 immediately recasts that spending as a good loan multiplied by God.
The expiatory meal is measured by the average of what one feeds one's own family, and inability triggers a nonfinancial alternative; it directly grounds giving in household support and actual means.

The ayah protects an orphan's property, commands full measure and weight with justice, and immediately limits responsibility to capacity, joining entrusted capital, an exact account, and means-sensitive obligation.
The warning to those who defraud introduces the opposite creditor-merchant posture from charitable reduction: an account is manipulated for the stronger party's gain.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving for themselves, the inverse of the creditor who voluntarily accepts less from a distressed debtor.
When giving by measure or weight, they cause others loss; this distinguishes imposed diminution of another's right from the claimant's own charitable remission.
What people withhold from God's bounty will be collared around them, turning retained surplus into a bodily burden rather than protected wealth.
Attaining righteousness requires spending from what one loves, extending the section's ordinary surplus measure by refusing to make generosity merely the disposal of what has little value.
Those called to spend may withhold, but their stinginess harms themselves; God is the Rich while they are the poor, reversing the apparent wealth hierarchy between creditor and needy recipient.
Consuming one another's wealth wrongfully, including by manipulating judgment, marks the boundary between enforcing a lawful principal and exploiting a debtor's property.
Mutually accepted trade is separated from consuming wealth wrongfully, supplying the transactional boundary needed beside the section's capital, loss, and creditor language.

A heavily burdened soul may call for help, yet none of its load is carried even by close kin; the boundary clarifies that merciful cancellation removes a liability rather than merely transferring its weight.
The correction to the mistaken wealth judgments in 89:15-16 begins with failure to honor the orphan, showing how abundance is tested by treatment of the vulnerable.
Failure to urge feeding the poor gives the concrete social consequence of reading restricted provision as humiliation rather than a claim on the community's means.
Greedily consuming inheritance adds an account-book wrong: the powerful take another's assigned wealth instead of preserving or relinquishing their own claim.
Excessive love of wealth completes the diagnosis behind harshness toward the poor and reluctance to lower a financial claim.
Although an injured party may claim an equivalent return, one who pardons and repairs has reward with God; it supplies the general claimant's ethic behind forgiving part of a debt.
Giving is to come from good earnings and produce, not defective property one would accept only reluctantly; charitable reduction is thus measured by honest value as well as amount.
People are told to spend from wealth over which God made them successors, weakening a creditor's claim to absolute ownership of the surplus he can use for relief.
Those who fear poverty are promised enrichment from God's bounty, another explicit movement from anticipated scarcity to divine sufficiency.
In the same family-law sphere as maintenance, separated spouses are each promised sufficiency from God's abundance, preventing present dependence from being treated as permanent.
All people are described as poor toward God while God alone is the Rich, placing the human creditor's temporary abundance inside a deeper debtor-like dependence.
Commerce whose decline is feared is listed among possessions that can hold people back, supplying the section's secondary commercial-loss sense with an explicit human fear of shrinking capital.
The offer of a trade that saves from punishment introduces a profitable divine transaction, reversing the section's image of loss in ordinary commerce.
That saving trade requires expenditure of wealth as well as personal striving, so capital apparently put down becomes the price of enduring gain.
Forgiveness and gardens are the settlement of the trade described in 61:10-11, completing its reversal of commercial loss.
Just balances are set for resurrection and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forward, giving the section's account book an exact standard of measure.
The Book and balance are sent so people may uphold justice, placing written claims and measured settlement under the same norm as the section's debt ledger.
God sends down the Book with truth and the balance, another pairing of written authority and measured judgment relevant to an accurately reduced claim.
Full measure and weighing with a straight balance state the commercial fairness that must govern the creditor's calculation before any voluntary remission begins.
Giving full measure and not joining those who cause loss establishes the fair commercial baseline from which the section's claimant may freely reduce his own right.
Weighing with a straight balance supplies the exact instrument for the account continued from 26:181.
Diminishing other people's goods is forbidden, distinguishing wrongful subtraction from lowering one's own claim for a debtor's benefit.
Shuʿayb commands full measure and weight and forbids diminishing people's possessions, a direct commercial boundary around the section's language of capital deduction.
Shuʿayb sees his people in prosperity yet warns them not to diminish measure or weight, showing that abundance can produce oppressive accounting rather than merciful relief.
The command to give full measure and weight with justice and not deprive people of their goods completes the fair-account scene begun in 11:84.
The responsibility of family maintenance is tied to spending from one's wealth, helping identify the dependent obligations that precede giving from surplus.
Feeding on a day of hunger makes material straitness itself the setting for generosity, another qualified extension beyond giving only in ease.
The near orphan is the first recipient named in that hunger scene, keeping family vulnerability inside the giver's calculation.
The destitute person in the dust completes the scene of aid directed to the most visibly constricted condition.
Harshly repelling the orphan is a social counterpart to the creditor who presses someone without power; it supplies a specific condemned posture toward vulnerability.
Refusal even to urge feeding the poor completes the withholding posture introduced in 107:2 and opposes remission as charity.
